headline: 80 feet on the Klondike lumps: bluefin in the slot, sea bass to 4 pounds on Wreck 3402
subhead: Steady high pressure is holding the tuna pattern together while the bottom bite grinds on like it always does in late July.
body_markdown:
Eighty feet. That's the number that's been in my book all week, written next to a set of coordinates on the western edge of the Klondike where the lumps rise up out of the mud and hold bait like a bowl holds water. Bluefin have been sitting right on top of that structure, marking thick from 50 down to 65 feet, and if you can get a spreader bar or a green machine daisy chain through that layer without a bluefish shredding it first, you're in business. Slot fish, mostly — 28 to 45 inch class — which is exactly what the recreational fishery wants right now with the trophy closure still in effect from July 3rd. Nobody's complaining about that. A 40-inch bluefin on 50-pound gear is still a workout on a July afternoon with the sun beating down and no wind to speak of.

That no-wind part matters. We called this one — said the flat-weather window would hold 48 to 72 hours out, and here we are, still sitting on glass most mornings out of Manasquan. That kind of stability doesn't happen twice in a July. It's building a real temperature break out past the Mud Hole and into the canyon approaches, warm surface water pushing into the high 70s, and that's dragging the bluefin bite further inshore than you'd expect for this time of year. Normally I'm sending guys 40-plus miles to find this action. This week some of it's showing up 25 miles off Manasquan Inlet, right on the Klondike structure, which is a gift if you don't want to burn the extra fuel and time to reach Hudson or Wilmington.

Yellowfin are still out at the canyons doing what they do when the water sets up right — Hudson, Wilmington, Washington, all producing on the troll with a mix of Ilanders and horse ballyhoo, and chunking butterflied bunker on the drift once you find the temp break. That's a longer run than most of my regulars want to make midweek, but if you've got the range and the fuel budget, it's the most consistent program on the entire coast right now. Mahi are riding shotgun on that trip too — any floating junk, any weed line drifting along the shelf, worth a few casts with a small popper or a chunk bait under a balloon. Nothing giant, mostly schoolies in the 3 to 8 pound range, but they eat and they're fun on light spinning gear while you wait on a tuna bite to develop.

Back inshore, where most of my trips actually happen, the bottom fishing has been the one thing I can set my watch to. Wreck 3402 — that's one of the numbers I don't hand out easy, sitting in about 80 feet off the Barnegat Ridge complex — has been holding jumbo sea bass all month. Fish to 4 pounds coming up on Gulp Grubs in white and chartreuse, tipped with a squid strip, fished on a high-low rig with 6-ounce bank sinkers to hold bottom in the current. The morning bite has been best on the last two hours of the incoming tide, before the sun gets too high and pushes the biggest fish deeper into the wreckage. Sea Girt Reef and Axel Carlson are producing too, though the average size runs smaller — good eating fish in the 14 to 16 inch range, plenty of them, but you have to sort through some shorts to find the keepers.

Shrewsbury Rocks has been quieter than I'd like this week. The porgy and sea bass are there, but the current's been running funny with these long stretches of settled weather — slack tides that don't move much water, which makes for a lazier bite. I fished it Tuesday and worked hard for a limit of sea bass, nothing like the Barnegat Ridge wrecks where the fish are stacked and hungry. If you're choosing between the two right now, I'd lean Ridge every time.

Triple Wrecks has been a mixed bag — some tog showing early, which is unusual for late July, probably fish that never left the structure through the warm months because there's enough current and bait to keep them comfortable. Nothing to build a trip around yet, but worth a rod in the spread if you're anchored up there working sea bass. Green crab on a jig head, dropped right into the wreckage, has picked at a few 3 and 4 pound tog between sea bass bites.

No bonito or false albacore reports out of our waters yet, though the water's warming in that direction and the southern New England boys are watching for the first scout schools any day now. When those show, they tend to work their way down the coast toward Shrewsbury Rocks and the reef line eventually, so it's on my radar for August.

Looking ahead, I'd bank on this high-pressure window holding through the weekend — the pattern's been stable enough that I'm not seeing anything in the setup that suggests a hard wind shift is imminent. That means the Klondike bluefin bite should keep producing on the lumps, and the sea bass on Wreck 3402 and the Barnegat Ridge wrecks should stay steady as long as the tides keep moving water through the structure. If I had one trip this week, I'd run the Ridge early on the incoming for sea bass, then swing out toward the Klondike lumps midday to see if the bluefin are still holding at 80 feet. That's the play — inshore insurance with an offshore shot on the same tank of gas.
